## TL;DR

Reviewed user-facing copy in the web app, mobile Hub, and macOS Hub. Replaced a web connection error that exposed a shell command with a plain instruction, and replaced “HTTP” with “error code” in the macOS server-address error. Added an assertion for the web wording and documented the review in `docs/qa/2026-11-copy-review.md`.

## Work and rationale

The review began with a search for technical terms likely to leak from implementation into product copy: endpoint, payload, worktree, bootstrap, artifact, provisioning, runtime, and HTTP. I inspected matches in context because many hits were comments, type names, test fixtures, or advanced developer controls rather than text regular users encounter.

The clearest web issue was the network failure message in the API wrapper. It told users to restart the server with a command. The app already distinguishes a server that is unreachable from one that is merely slow, and its recovery banner can show a restart action. I changed the generic instruction to “Start the server, then reload,” preserving the recognizable “RepoOS server” term while removing command-line jargon. The recovery view remains responsible for the more specific restart control.

The macOS health-check error included an HTTP status code and called it “HTTP.” The numeric code is useful for support, but the protocol acronym does not help someone decide what to do. The revised message says “error code” and asks the user to check that the address points to a RepoOS server. It retains the code and names the destination clearly.

The mobile app’s server discovery and HTTPS messages were already direct and actionable, so I left them alone. Other terms such as worktree and artifact are used on task or developer screens where the underlying Git/build concept matters. A global rename would risk obscuring meaningful distinctions. The review note records these boundaries and the observed vocabulary.

## Approaches tried

I searched the web, mobile, and macOS source trees for likely infrastructure jargon, then narrowed the results to literal strings and inspected the surrounding UI or error handling. I checked tests for the web outage wording and found the recovery-banner test that classifies refused connections. I updated its shared fixture string and added a focused assertion that the user-facing copy names the RepoOS server, gives a simple next step, and does not expose the `repoos serve` command.

I also reviewed mobile HTTPS guidance and macOS health and navigation errors. This was more useful than mechanically replacing every HTTP or worktree reference: some strings are aimed at advanced users, while protocol names are necessary in security guidance.

## Challenges and blockers

The main judgment call was where technical vocabulary is genuinely confusing versus useful in context. “Server” is the consistent name for the RepoOS instance, while “project” refers to the repository served by it. “Runner” and “agent” refer to different product roles and should not be conflated. Similarly, the HTTP status number remains in the macOS error because the acronym can be removed without losing diagnostic value.

This was a copy-focused task and did not require launching a browser or changing layout. I did not open a visible browser. The task check is the validation gate; any check result should be taken from the run itself rather than inferred from code inspection.

## Key learnings

The most helpful error copy is consistent with the action the interface offers. A generic fetch error should explain that the RepoOS server cannot be reached and point to a simple recovery step; it should not require users to know a terminal command. A status number can remain when it supports troubleshooting, provided the sentence around it uses ordinary language.

Search results need context. Many occurrences of words such as “endpoint,” “payload,” and “worktree” are internal identifiers or advanced workflow details, not copy defects. Focused edits preserve domain distinctions and avoid making technical screens less precise. The November review document captures what was checked, what changed, and why other terms were retained.
